## Where We're Headed

*From "what is an intelligent system" to what actual users report when it fails them.*

1. **What counts as "AI"** — a working definition of intelligent everyday applications
2. **AI application examples** — six real, documented systems you already use
3. **The Eiband et al. study** — 35,448 app reviews reveal what actually goes wrong for users
4. **Design implications** — what HCI researchers now recommend based on real user reports

## What Makes an App "Intelligent"?

*A working definition, borrowed from the HCI literature.*

::: {.callout}
An intelligent system "embodies one or more capabilities that have traditionally been associated more strongly with humans than with computers, such as the abilities to perceive, interpret, learn, use language, reason, plan, and decide."

— Jameson & Riedl (2011), as adopted by Eiband et al. (2019)
:::

**What this looks like in practice**

Algorithmic decision-making has quietly permeated the apps people use every day: it selects what information is relevant, decides which content users do or do not see, draws inferences from behavior, and shapes what users do next.

## Example 1 · Netflix Recommender System

*Personalization at the center of a $1-billion-a-year business decision.*

**How it works**

Netflix uses a variety of supervised and unsupervised machine learning techniques to personalize recommendations for each account — ranking titles, curating rows, and even selecting which thumbnail image to show a given viewer.

| | |
|---|---|
| **80%** | of hours streamed on Netflix are influenced by the recommender system |
| **$1B+** | estimated annual savings from personalization and recommendations |

*Gomez-Uribe, C. A., & Hunt, N. (2015). The Netflix Recommender System. ACM TMIS, 6(4).*

## Example 2 · Google Maps Routing

*Classical algorithms and deep learning, working together.*

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Google Maps' turn-by-turn routing is still built on **Dijkstra's classical shortest-path algorithm (1959)** — but the map data feeding that algorithm is kept current with deep learning and computer vision, which scans Street View imagery to automatically detect addresses, business names, and speed-limit signs.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Route-finding**: Dijkstra's algorithm computes the fastest path across the road network.

**Map maintenance**: Deep learning reads addresses and signage from millions of Street View images.
:::
:::

*Ibarz, J. (2017). Updating Google Maps with Deep Learning and Street View. Google AI Blog.*

## Example 3 · Facebook News Feed

*The most-studied curation algorithm in HCI research.*

Facebook's News Feed is algorithmically curated based on user behavior such as likes, comments, and time spent — deciding which of your friends' and pages' posts you actually see.

::: {.callout}
**A landmark finding:** Eslami et al. (2015) found that 62.5% of participants did not know Facebook algorithmically curates their feed at all — they assumed friends and family were simply choosing not to post, or were actively hiding content from them.
:::

*Eslami, M., et al. (2015). "I Always Assumed that I Wasn't Really that Close to [Her]." CHI '15.*

## Examples 4 & 5 · Two Faces of AI in Gmail

*One system decides what you don't see. The other helps you write what you do.*

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.tag-midnight}
**Spam & Threat Filtering**

Gmail's ML classifiers block more than 99.9% of spam, phishing, and malware — filtering roughly 100 million additional spam messages a day since Google added TensorFlow-based models.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**Smart Compose**

Launched in 2018, Smart Compose predicts sentence completions as you type. Google reports the feature saves users over **2 billion characters** of typing every week.
:::
:::
:::

## Example 6 · Face ID

*Biometric AI: intelligence you interact with in under a second.*

Apple's TrueDepth camera projects and reads over 30,000 infrared dots to build a 3D depth map of the user's face, compared against enrolled data entirely on-device inside the Secure Enclave.

::: {.callout}
**1 in 1,000,000** — the probability a random person could unlock a given iPhone with Face ID, vs. 1 in 50,000 for Touch ID. Apple's white paper also discloses that the false-match rate is measurably higher for identical twins, siblings, and children under 13.
:::

*Apple Inc. (2017). Face ID Security (white paper).*

## "When People and Algorithms Meet" {background-color="#BA0C2F"}

::: {.kicker}
A CLOSER LOOK
:::

*Eiband, Völkel, Buschek, Cook & Hussmann (2019) — what 35,448 real app reviews reveal about everyday AI failures.*

## Study Overview & Methodology

*IUI '19 · A large-scale, empirical look at three of our six applications.*

::: {.callout}
"The complex nature of intelligent systems... poses difficult challenges for HCI... [yet] there is yet little empirical evidence on specific problems users face in such systems in everyday use."
:::

| | |
|---|---|
| **35,448** | Google Play reviews scraped across Facebook, Netflix & Google Maps |
| **7,559** | reviews with negative sentiment kept for detailed topic-modeling analysis |
| **286** | follow-up survey participants describing real coping strategies |

*Method: sentiment analysis + LDA topic modeling on reviews rated ≤ 3 stars, manually labeled, then validated with an online survey.*

## Facebook: What Users Reported {.smaller}

*274 reviews, 3 core problems — mostly about the curation algorithm itself.*

| Problem | Reviews | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Biased content curation | 117 | "Cowards, censuring videos... why not let people post what they want?!" |
| Selective composition & ranking | 81 | "...you know what I miss, seeing actual post from friends. Not ads..." |
| Insufficient options for AI components | 76 | Users wanted to remove features like "People You May Know" |

## Netflix: What Users Reported {.smaller}

*694 reviews across four problem categories — the widest spread of the three apps.*

| Category | What users said |
|---|---|
| Knowledge base | "For a film lover myself, it's grown stale." Outdated, incomplete, or biased selection. |
| Algorithm | "You guys don't even give good recommendation anymore." Mismatched suggestions. |
| User choice | "I need more than a still photo and search keywords to decide." |
| User feedback | "How am I supposed to know if I should watch it if every movie is a match?" |

## Google Maps: What Users Reported {.smaller}

*1,072 reviews — over a third of all Maps reviews analyzed described a core AI problem.*

| Category | What users said |
|---|---|
| Knowledge base | "My location appears to shift a kilometre or more in seconds." |
| Algorithm | "Keeps adding completely random routes... 10 minutes extra travel time." |
| User choice | "Then, without telling me, just puts me back on the quickest route." |
| User feedback | "Google have failed to respond to requests to fix the flaw." |

## The Four-Stage Problem Framework {background-color="#BA0C2F"}

*Across all three apps, problems cluster at the same four points in the algorithmic pipeline.*

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'theme':'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor':'#7A0A22','primaryTextColor':'#fff','primaryBorderColor':'#C0AC7E','lineColor':'#C0AC7E'}}}%%
flowchart LR
    KB["1. Knowledge Base
    Input data is wrong,
    missing, or outdated"] --> AL["2. Algorithm
    The inference itself
    misfires"]
    AL --> UC["3. User Choice
    No way to override,
    customize, or turn off"]
    UC --> UF["4. User Feedback
    Corrections and ratings
    go nowhere"]
    style KB fill:#7A0A22,color:#fff
    style AL fill:#7A0A22,color:#fff
    style UC fill:#7A0A22,color:#fff
    style UF fill:#C0AC7E,color:#333
```

::: {.callout}
This framework doesn't just diagnose Facebook, Netflix, and Google Maps — it's a lens you can point at any AI-powered application to locate exactly where its user experience is breaking down.
:::

## Coping Strategies: How Users Route Around AI

*When the system doesn't work for them, users find their own workarounds.*

- **Search manually** — Netflix users searched the catalog directly; Maps users navigated without the app
- **Get recommendations elsewhere** — asked friends or checked outside rating sites
- **Control content directly** — Facebook users unfriended, unfollowed, or marked ads as spam
- **Abandon the app's suggestion** — Google Maps users ignored rerouting mid-drive

## Five Design Implications {background-color="#BA0C2F"}

*What Eiband et al. recommend, directly grounded in what real users asked for.*

1. **Let users stay in control** — suggestions should inform, not override
2. **Provide fine-grained control** — more specific options than a single on/off toggle
3. **Explain interactively** — let users try settings and see the effect live
4. **Allow AI to be switched off** — support opting out of algorithmic curation entirely
5. **Honor expressive feedback** — move beyond binary thumbs up/down

## Implication 1 · Let Users Stay in Control

*Control issues reoccurred across every single app the researchers studied.*

::: {.callout}
"Users appreciate suggestions but want to make the final decision themselves... the system should not alter a decision that has been made by a user."
:::

**The clearest example: Google Maps rerouting.** Both the app-review analysis and the follow-up survey turned up the same complaint: users manually selected a scenic route, and Google Maps silently switched them back to the fastest route mid-drive. This is a subtle but important shift from most explainable-AI research, which has focused on explaining the *how and why* of a decision, not the item itself.

## Implications 2 & 3 · Granular Control, Interactive Explanation

*Binary toggles aren't enough — and static explanations aren't either.*

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**Fine-grained control options**

Google Maps users wanted a truck-routing mode; Netflix users wanted mood-based filtering; Facebook users wanted to weight posts by how often they message a person.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Explain interactively**

Participants wanted to try different settings and see the algorithm's output change — for example, live-toggling the Facebook feed between chronological and algorithmically curated order.
:::
:::

## Implications 4 & 5 · An Off-Switch, and Feedback That Counts

*Sometimes the best support is the option to disengage from the algorithm entirely.*

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.tag-midnight}
**Turn intelligence on and off**

A striking number of participants used these apps' non-intelligent features on purpose: navigating without Maps' routing, searching Netflix manually, or visiting a friend's Facebook profile directly.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Honor expressive feedback**

Netflix's binary thumbs up/down was one of the most heavily criticized features in the dataset. Users wanted the old five-star system back.
:::
:::

## The Big Finding: Trust in Humans Still Wins {background-color="#7A0A22"}

*Even in low-risk, everyday contexts — not just high-stakes medical or legal decisions.*

::: {.callout}
"Our results indicate a tendency to favour human over algorithmic decision-making, not only in sensitive domains but also in comparably low-risk intelligent everyday applications."
:::

**Netflix**: Users mostly chose what to watch by asking friends or checking outside rating sites — not by trusting Netflix's own matching score.

**Google Maps**: Some users estimated their own arrival time instead of trusting the app's ETA, because their own estimate matched reality better.

## Everyday AI, Through the HAI Lens {.smaller}

*This isn't a new topic for the course — it's the same questions, wearing everyday clothes.*

| | |
|---|---|
| **Human-in-the-loop** | Google Maps' silent rerouting is an out-of-the-loop failure: users had no chance to approve the change. |
| **Direct manipulation vs. delegation** | Manually searching Netflix instead of trusting recommendations is the 1997 Shneiderman–Maes debate, replayed by ordinary users. |
| **Explanations, not just predictions** | Eiband et al.'s finding — describe the item, not the algorithm — challenges a decade of explainable-AI research. |
| **The role of humans in AI** | User feedback is training data. When Netflix ignores that signal, it degrades the system's own knowledge base. |

## Discussion Questions {background-color="#003B5C" .smaller}

*Bring your answers to at least one of these to class.*

1. Pick an app you use daily that wasn't covered today. Using the four-stage framework, where does it most often fail you?
2. Eiband et al. found users want explanations of the recommended item, not the algorithm's reasoning. Do you agree — or can you think of a situation where you'd genuinely want to know why?
3. Netflix's move from five-star ratings to thumbs up/down was presumably tested and shipped deliberately. Why might a company make a change its own most engaged users clearly dislike?
4. If "letting users turn off AI entirely" is good design, why do so few apps actually offer that option?

## Key Takeaways

*What six real applications and one landmark study teach us about designing everyday AI.*

- AI isn't a future technology to prepare for — it's already the recommender behind 80% of what you watch, the router deciding your commute, and the filter deciding which emails you never see.
- User problems with everyday AI cluster at four predictable points: bad input data, a misfiring algorithm, no way to override it, and feedback that goes nowhere.
- When AI gets it wrong, users don't wait for a fix — they route around it. Every workaround is a design failure hiding in plain sight.
- Across low-risk, everyday contexts, people still tend to trust their own judgment, or another human's, over an algorithm's.
